concept.name: Calmar ratio
concept.definition: A drawdown-based performance measure: the average annual (compound) rate of return over a trailing 36-month window divided by the maximum drawdown over the same window, computed monthly. Created by Terry W. Young in 1991 for evaluating commodity trading advisors.
concept.intuition: It prices performance in units of worst pain: how much annual return do you get for each unit of the deepest hole the strategy digs in three years?
concept.mechanics: Compute the compound annualized return over the last 36 months and divide by the absolute maximum drawdown measured on that window; recalculate monthly so the ratio evolves gradually. A close relative, the MAR ratio, uses the full track record from inception instead of the rolling window.
concept.failure_modes: The 36-month window makes it backward-window-dependent: a crisis rolling out of the window can improve the ratio without any change in the strategy, and young funds without a full window are unevaluable. Like all drawdown ratios it is driven by a single worst episode.
concept.misconceptions: Calmar and MAR ratios are not identical — Calmar uses a rolling 36-month window while MAR uses inception-to-date data — and a high Calmar can coexist with mediocre recent performance if the window's drawdown was shallow.
concept.example: A CTA with a 15% compound annual return and a 10% maximum drawdown over the trailing 36 months has a Calmar ratio of 1.5.
